facts.text: The greater crested tern announces its territory with a loud, raucous, crow-like "kerrak" call, especially around its breeding grounds.
facts.quote: The greater crested tern is highly vocal, especially at its breeding grounds. The territorial advertising call is a loud, raucous, crow-like kerrak.

facts.text: Fish make up nearly 90% of its diet, with the rest including cephalopods, crustaceans, insects, agamid lizards and green turtle hatchlings.
facts.quote: Fish are the main food of the greater crested tern, found to make up nearly 90% of all prey items with the remainder including cephalopods, crustaceans and insects. Unusual vertebrate prey included agamid lizards and green turtle hatchlings.

facts.text: This adaptable bird follows trawlers, even at night, and during the fishing season trawl discards can make up 70% of its diet.
facts.quote: This tern actively follows trawlers, including at night, and during the fishing season trawl discards can constitute 70% of its diet.

facts.text: In courtship, a male flies around the colony with a fish in its beak, calling loudly, before the pair settle and the gift is exchanged.
facts.quote: One bird flies around the colony with a fish in its beak, calling loudly; its partner may also fly, but the pair eventually settle and the gift is exchanged.

facts.text: The largest documented colony, with 13,000 to 15,000 pairs, is in the Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia.
facts.quote: the largest documented colony, with 13,000 to 15,000 pairs, is in the Gulf of Carpentaria in northern Australia

facts.text: Parents can't recognise their own eggs or newly hatched chicks, but can distinguish their chicks by the time they are two days old.
facts.quote: Parents do not recognize their own eggs or newly hatched chicks, but are able to distinguish their chicks by the time they are two days-old, shortly before they begin to wander from the nest.

facts.text: Young terns fledge after 38 to 40 days but stay dependent on their parents for about four months.
facts.quote: The young terns fledge after 38 to 40 days, but remain dependent on the parents after leaving the colony until they are about four months old.

facts.text: With a stable population of more than 500,000 birds, the species faces no global conservation concerns despite local declines.
facts.quote: There are no global conservation concerns for this bird, which has a stable total population of more than 500,000 individuals.
